Content:
Let [MATH: n] be a positive integer. A function [MATH: B: \Bbb R^n\times \Bbb R^n \to \Bbb R] is said to be a bilinear form if there is an [MATH: n\times n] matrix [MATH: A] such that

Content:
[MATH: B(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A\mathbf{y}, \qquad \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \Bbb R^n.]

Content:
Suppose, for example, that [MATH: [1|2; 3|4]] To evaluate the bilinear form [MATH: B(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{y}] when [MATH: [1; 2]] and [MATH: [− 1; 1]] we substitute these vectors in the above expression as follows

Content:
[MATH: B(x, y)|= x^{T}Ay; = [1|2][1|2; 3|4][− 1; 1]; = [7|10][− 1; 1]; = 3.]

Content:
To write down our bilinear form [MATH: B(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})] above in terms of vector components

Content:
[MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}]]

Content:
we proceed as follows:

Content:
[MATH: B(x, y)|= x^{T}Ay; = [x_{1}|x_{2}][1|2; 3|4][y_{1}; y_{2}]; = [x_{1}|x_{2}][y_{1} + 2y_{2}; 3y_{1} + 4y_{2}]; = x_{1}(y_{1} + 2y_{2}) + x_{2}(3y_{1} + 4y_{2}); = x_{1}y_{1} + 2x_{1}y_{2} + 3x_{2}y_{1} + 4x_{2}y_{2}]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let [MATH: n] be a positive integer. A function

Content:
[MATH: f: \Bbb R^n \to \Bbb R]

Content:
is a linear form (or linear functional) if there is a row-vector

Content:
[MATH: [a_{1}|a_{2}|⋯|a_{n}]]

Content:
such that for any [MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}; ⋮; x_{n}]] we have

Content:
[MATH: f(x)|= ax; = [a_{1}|a_{2}|⋯|a_{n}] ⋅ [x_{1}; x_{2}; ⋮; x_{n}]; = a_{1}x_{1} + a_{2}x_{2} + … + a_{n}x_{n}.]

Content:
For example, let [MATH: f(\mathbf{x})] be the linear form defined on [MATH: \Bbb R^2] by [MATH: f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{a} \mathbf{x},] where [MATH: [3|− 2]]

Content:
Suppose we want to evaluate [MATH: f(\mathbf{x})] at [MATH: [1; − 1]] Then, we simply substitute [MATH: [1; − 1]] and obtain

Content:
[MATH: f(x)|= ax; = [3|− 2] ⋅ [1; − 1]; = 3 ⋅ 1 + (− 2) ⋅ (− 1); = 3 + 2; = 5.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Evaluating a Linear Form

Example Prompt:
The linear form [MATH: f(\mathbf{x})] is defined as [MATH: f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{a} \mathbf{x},] where [MATH: [3|0|4]] Evaluate the function when [MATH: [− 5; 8; 5]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Substituting [MATH: [− 5; 8; 5]] we obtain

[MATH: f(x)|= ax; = [3|0|4] ⋅ [− 5; 8; 5]; = 3 ⋅ (− 5) + 0 ⋅ 8 + 4 ⋅ 5; = − 15 + 0 + 20; = 5.]

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: Bilinear Forms

Content:
Let [MATH: n] be a positive integer. A function [MATH: B: \Bbb R^n\times \Bbb R^n \to \Bbb R] is said to be a bilinear form if there is an [MATH: n\times n] matrix [MATH: A] such that

Content:
[MATH: B(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A\mathbf{y}, \qquad \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \Bbb R^n.]

Content:
Suppose, for example, that [MATH: [1|2; 3|4]] To evaluate the bilinear form [MATH: B(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{y}] when [MATH: [1; 2]] and [MATH: [− 1; 1]] we substitute these vectors in the above expression as follows

Content:
[MATH: B(x, y)|= x^{T}Ay; = [1|2][1|2; 3|4][− 1; 1]; = [7|10][− 1; 1]; = 3.]

Content:
To write down our bilinear form [MATH: B(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})] above in terms of vector components

Content:
[MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}]]

Content:
we proceed as follows:

Content:
[MATH: B(x, y)|= x^{T}Ay; = [x_{1}|x_{2}][1|2; 3|4][y_{1}; y_{2}]; = [x_{1}|x_{2}][y_{1} + 2y_{2}; 3y_{1} + 4y_{2}]; = x_{1}(y_{1} + 2y_{2}) + x_{2}(3y_{1} + 4y_{2}); = x_{1}y_{1} + 2x_{1}y_{2} + 3x_{2}y_{1} + 4x_{2}y_{2}]

---

Item 6 — Example: Evaluating a Bilinear Form

Example Prompt:
Consider the the bilinear form [MATH: B(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}),] given by

Evaluate [MATH: B(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})] when [MATH: [1; 1; − 1]] and [MATH: [− 2; 2; 1]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We are given that

[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}; x_{3}]] and [MATH: [y_{1}; y_{2}; y_{3}]]

Substituting these into the bilinear expression, we obtain

[MATH: B(x, y)|= 2x_{1}y_{2} − x_{2}y_{2} + 3x_{2}y_{3} − x_{3}y_{1}; = 2 ⋅ 1 ⋅ 2 − 1 ⋅ 2 + 3 ⋅ 1 ⋅ 1 − (− 1) ⋅ (− 2); = 4 − 2 + 3 − 2; = 3.]

Item 9 — Example: Writing Down a Bilinear Form Given Its Matrix

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Method 1

Each entry [MATH: a_{ij}] of [MATH: A] corresponds to the term [MATH: a_{ij}x_i y_j] in the expression of the bilinear form:

[MATH: x^{T}Ay|= 2x_{1}y_{1} + (− 1)x_{1}y_{2} + 3x_{2}y_{1} + (− 2)x_{2}y_{2}; = 2x_{1}y_{1} − x_{1}y_{2} + 3x_{2}y_{1} − 2x_{2}y_{2}]

Method 2

To write down a bilinear form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

[MATH: x^{T}Ay|= [x_{1}|x_{2}][2|− 1; 3|− 2][y_{1}; y_{2}]; = [x_{1}|x_{2}][2y_{1} − y_{2}; 3y_{1} − 2y_{2}]; = x_{1}(2y_{1} − y_{2}) + x_{2}(3y_{1} − 2y_{2}); = 2x_{1}y_{1} − x_{1}y_{2} + 3x_{2}y_{1} − 2x_{2}y_{2}]

Item 15 — Tutorial: Properties of Bilinear Forms

Content:
Suppose [MATH: A] is an [MATH: n\times n] matrix. Then, it readily follows that the function [MATH: B: \Bbb R^n\times \Bbb R^n \to \Bbb R] defined as

Content:
[MATH: B(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \, \mathbf{y}, \qquad \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \Bbb R^n,]

Content:
is linear in each argument separately. That's the reason why we call them bilinear.

Content:
- For [MATH: \mathbf{y}] fixed, all [MATH: \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \Bbb R^n,] and any real constant [MATH: c], linearity in the first argument means the following:

Content:
[MATH: B(u + v, y)|= B(u, y) + B(v, y); B(cu, y)|= cB(u, y)]

Content:
- For [MATH: \mathbf{x}] fixed, all [MATH: \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{z} \in \Bbb R^n,] and any real constant [MATH: c], linearity in the second argument means the following:

Content:
[MATH: B(x, w + z)|= B(x, w) + B(x, z); B(x, cw)|= cB(x, w)]
